title: Create competitor comparison sheets for your sales team
description: A system that keeps a competitor comparison sheet current for your sales team by combining public research with your own win-loss notes.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

hubspot.title: HubSpot
hubspot.content: A CRM and marketing platform used by sales, marketing, and customer success teams. Common target for AI automations — students connect it to draft outreach, enrich contacts, or sync data with other tools.

workflow.title: Workflow
workflow.content: A multi-step process Claude runs to accomplish a goal — for example: read emails → filter by topic → summarize → post to Slack. Workflows can be run manually or on a schedule.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

personal-knowledge-base.title: Personal Knowledge Base
personal-knowledge-base.content: A store of your own accumulated knowledge — notes, decisions, references — organized so an AI can search and use it. The difference from a pile of documents: structure and maintenance. Level 2 builds one as a wiki.

children.text: A battlecard nobody has touched since the last competitor pricing change misleads a rep mid-deal instead of helping them. [Anthropic's Claude Academy](https://academy.claude.com/courses/claude-101/claude-in-action-use-cases-by-role) lists building battlecard libraries as a standard sales [workflow](#tooltip-workflow), treated as ongoing upkeep rather than a document written once and left alone.

This system pulls public research on a named competitor and combines it with your team's own win-loss notes, then produces a comparison sheet covering differentiators, likely objections, and talk tracks. The strongest sheets pair outside-in research with inside-out evidence from deals your team has won and lost.

Run it as a recurring paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) whenever a competitor changes, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill) your team reuses, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that checks for stale sections and flags them for review. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) until a named person signs off on a claim.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your competitors, where your win-loss notes live, and who approves a claim before it's added.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that keeps a competitor comparison sheet current for my sales team. Ask me questions, one at a time, about which competitors come up in deals, where our win-loss notes live, and who approves a claim before it's added. When you have what you need, write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming an approver up front stops the sheet from filling with unverified claims later.

items: Who signs off before a claim goes live.
How often each competitor changes enough to justify a refresh.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are your CRM or win-loss notes (Salesforce, [HubSpot](#tooltip-hubspot), a shared doc), public research (competitor sites, G2), and your [knowledge base](#tooltip-personal-knowledge-base) ([Notion](#tooltip-notion), Confluence). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real competitor. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Update the sheet for [competitor] using the latest public information and our own win-loss notes.

Context: [Paste our core differentiators, where win-loss notes live, and the sections this sheet covers: differentiators, objections, talk tracks, landmines.]

Rules:
- Mark every claim sourced (link) or internal (named deal).
- Never state pricing or features as fact without a current source.
- Flag anything unverified in the last 90 days.
- No pricing claims go in without sign-off.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the sourced-or-internal split keeps a stale public claim from sitting next to a live one unmarked.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every claim marked, nothing on pricing without sign-off?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong and fold each correction into the rules so the fix sticks for next time.

items: Add a "landmines" section of early-deal questions that expose a weak fit fast.
Track which talk tracks correlate with actual wins.
Flag public pricing changes as soon as they post.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric), not a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each comparison sheet update, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, competitor, claims added, claims flagged unverified, and sign-off status. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log makes a skipped sign-off visible fast.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. After a few refresh cycles it shows which competitors need the most attention and whether sign-off is happening at all. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few cycles straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that fails again and again is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. A sheet built once and never revisited becomes a liability, so give the refresh one named owner or it quietly goes stale.
